rejected.title: Lower of cost and net realisable value
card: Inventory is reported at the lower of its cost and its net realisable value (NRV). This stops inventory being shown at more than the business can expect to recover.
NRV
the expected selling price less any costs needed to make the sale, such as delivery or sales commission.
If NRV is below cost, the inventory is written down to NRV. The write-down is recorded as an expense, and the inventory account falls.
If NRV is above cost, inventory stays at cost. A gain is not recorded until the goods are sold.
rejected.remember: Compare cost with NRV and use the lower. Write down a fall, but never value inventory above cost.

a.q: Which description matches net realisable value?
opts: Expected selling price less the costs of making the sale
Expected selling price plus the costs of making the sale
The price the business paid, plus freight in
The price the business would pay to replace the goods
a.why: NRV is what the business can expect to recover from a sale after selling costs are taken off. Adding the selling costs is wrong, because they reduce the amount the business keeps.
a.clue: Think of what is left after the costs of selling.

b.q: Ravi's Cycles in Geelong holds 10 bikes costing $400 each. Each can be sold for $480, but selling costs are $100 per bike. At what value are the 10 bikes reported?
opts: $3,800, the NRV of $380 per bike
$4,000, the cost of $400 per bike
$4,800, the selling price of $480 per bike
$800, the profit margin of $80 per bike
b.why: NRV per bike is $480 less $100, which is $380. This is below the cost of $400, so the bikes are written down to $3,800 in total. Cost of $4,000 is tempting because the selling price is above cost, but selling costs must come off first.
b.clue: Take selling costs off the price before comparing it with cost.

also_right: $3,800, the selling price less cost per bike

problems.detail: Two options give the same correct total of $3,800. The distractor '$3,800, the selling price less cost per bike' is ambiguous. If 'cost' means the $400 purchase cost, the working is wrong ($80 per bike) but the figure is still right. If 'cost' means the selling cost, it is simply correct. A student who calculates correctly can be marked wrong for picking the reported value the question asks for. Replace it with a distractor that has a different figure, such as $800 (selling price less cost, $80 per bike).

'Never write up a gain' is stronger than the card and could mislead. Under AASB 102, a previous write-down can be reversed, back up to original cost, if NRV later rises. What is never allowed is reporting inventory above cost. Safer wording: 'never value inventory above cost.'

The remember line's 'never write up a gain' overstates the rule, since reversals of earlier write-downs are allowed up to cost.
